name: flux-wc
description: Lines, words, bytes and characters per file -- wc for records.
author: takakix2
notes:
Lines, words, bytes and characters, as Flux signals: one record per file (lines, words, bytes, chars, max_line, utf8), in input order. Counts the files named, the files Flux records on stdin point to (flux-ls | flux-wc), or the text on stdin itself. Files are read in parallel. -l / -w / -c / -m / -L (as wc has them) ask for some counts only, and lines or bytes alone are counted without decoding the text -- as fast as GNU wc -l. Linux, macOS and Windows.

Which stdin it is, is decided by the first non-empty line: a JSON object with v and path means records (directories among them are skipped and counted on stderr); anything else is text, counted as one record with path null. --text always counts the text (to count the lines of a Flux stream itself). lines is the number of newlines, as wc -l counts it: a last line without one is not counted. Words split where GNU wc splits them in a UTF-8 locale (Unicode white space with the vertical tab, without NEL). chars and max_line (the longest line, in characters) need UTF-8: content that is not is utf8: false with those two null, and the byte counts stay. No total unless --total (one count-total record). A file that cannot be read is null and said on stderr; nothing countable at all is exit 1. The library entry (run_in) takes stdin and writers explicitly and never exits the process. -l -w -c -m -L (alone or together, -lc) keep only those fields in the record; the others are left out, not null (null means could not count). Lines and bytes alone skip decoding (a newline byte never occurs inside a UTF-8 character); bytes alone of a regular file come from its size without reading, except a file that says size 0 (/proc), which is read. max_line is in characters, not display columns: GNU wc -L counts a wide character as 2 and a tab up to 8, so the two differ on Japanese text and tabs.
